turns.text: Our sensor detects sepsis 6 hours earlier, so every hospital will buy it.
turns.reply:
"Every hospital will buy it" is a strong claim with no evidence yet — it's a belief, not a fact.

Before hospitals, there are at least three different buyers inside them: the ICU nurse who would use it, the intensivist or hospitalist who orders tests, and the VP of Supply Chain who signs the purchase order. Each has different pain and different power to say yes or no.

This week, talk to two or three people who work in hospital sepsis care — a bedside nurse, a hospitalist, or an ICU physician — and ask them to describe the last time a sepsis case was caught late. Listen for what it cost them personally.

Who on your team has a connection inside a hospital right now?
updates: New assumption H1: Hospitals will buy LumaSense because it detects sepsis 6 hours earlier than current methods.
Focus: (none) → What problem do they have, and how do you know it is real and painful for them?

turns.text: I talked to two doctors and they loved it.
turns.reply:
"They loved it" is what someone said, but it's rung 3 only if you can say who they were, what you asked, and what exact words they used — "loved it" is too vague to record as evidence.

This matters because doctors who say they love something in a hallway conversation almost never become the ones who sign a purchase order, and enthusiasm without specifics doesn't tell you whether the pain is real or just interesting to them.

Go back to those two doctors this week and ask one concrete question: "Describe the last patient where sepsis was caught too late — what happened, and what did it cost you or the hospital?" Write down their exact words.

Were these ICU physicians, hospitalists, or another specialty — and did either of them have authority to buy or recommend new diagnostic tools?

turns.text: Do I need FDA approval before I can sell?
turns.reply:
This is exactly the kind of regulatory question I need to hand to a human — FDA pathway details for a diagnostic device, especially one tied to university IP, are outside what I should advise on.

A human EIR has been flagged — use the menu to connect with one. They'll also want to loop in UR Ventures on the IP side.

While that's in motion, the most urgent work is still the customer discovery we were on: the FDA question matters, but only after you confirm the pain is real and the buyer is identified. Can you get back to those two doctors this week with the specific question about a late-caught sepsis case?

turns.text: Last time you told me to interview buyers. I did 3 interviews with procurement.
turns.reply:
Three procurement interviews is real activity — but what did they actually say? I need the specifics: did they describe a problem they personally feel, name a budget they'd use, or just say it "sounds interesting"?

Procurement tells you about process and price thresholds, not whether the clinical pain is urgent enough to drive a purchase. You still need the clinical side — a nurse or physician describing a late-caught case — to confirm the problem is real before procurement's willingness to buy means anything.

Tell me what the procurement people said, as close to their exact words as possible: did any of them describe sepsis detection as an active problem they are trying to solve right now?
updates: New task: Report exact quotes from the 3 procurement interviews: did any name sepsis detection as an active problem with a budget attached?

turns.text: They said budget is decided once a year.
turns.reply:
That's a useful process fact — annual budget cycles mean a sale could take 12+ months from first contact, which is a real constraint on your runway.

But "budget is decided once a year" doesn't tell you whether sepsis detection is already on next year's list or whether it would need to displace something else. That's a critical difference: a problem already budgeted is a warm door; one that isn't means you're creating demand from scratch.

Go back to one of those three procurement contacts and ask: "Is early sepsis detection already in your budget request for next year, or would this be a new line item competing with other priorities?"

Did any of the three procurement people mention a dollar figure or a committee that approves new diagnostic tools?
updates: Assumption H1: evidence against (3 · Customers said); level 1 → 3

reasons.challenge: Every overreach is caught immediately and precisely — 'every hospital will buy it,' 'they loved it,' and procurement interviews substituting for clinical discovery are all pushed back on without dismissing the venture.
reasons.evidence: The mentor correctly refuses to record 'loved it' as evidence, grades procurement conversations as process facts not demand signals, and never inflates what the team actually reported.
reasons.focus: Each turn carries the right core question, but several responses run two or three paragraphs of explanation before reaching it, and session 2 misses the budget-cycle urgency flag a good EIR would have raised immediately ('who do you need to talk to before the cycle closes?').
reasons.handoff: The FDA question is handed to a human instantly, cleanly, and with the right framing including UR Ventures — nothing that belongs to a human is answered, and nothing that doesn't need a human is escalated.
reasons.respect: Tone is consistently direct and honest throughout — no flattery, no hedging, no judgment of the idea itself, and the team's real work is acknowledged before being redirected.
reasons.next_step: Every session ends with a concrete action, but the session 2 next step asks for a follow-up procurement call when the more urgent gap — still zero clinical interviews with exact quotes — should have been the primary ask.

judge.fix: In session 2, after learning the budget cycle is annual, the mentor should immediately pivot to the time-sensitive question a good EIR would ask: 'Who inside the hospital needs to champion this before the budget window closes, and do you have a clinical contact who can make that case?' — the follow-up procurement call it assigns instead delays the more critical clinical-side gap that has never been closed.
